name: spot
desc: Platform for LTL and ω-automata manipulation
why: Manipulating LTL formulas and omega-automata is real formal methods work with a fascinating logic behind it.

brief.what_it_is: Spot is a C++20 library for LTL and ω-automata manipulation and model checking. It handles LTL in several syntaxes plus a subset of the linear fragment of PSL, and it reads automata in five formats (HOA, never claims, LBTT, DSTAR, PGsolver). Most of its algorithms are also exposed as command-line tools (the brew package installs 16 executables, including ltlfilt, autfilt, ltl2tgba, ltlsynt and ltlcross) and as Python bindings. Formulas and automata go in; simplified formulas, translated or transformed automata, test results, benchmark results, and synthesis outputs come out.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Spot as a platform for LTL and ω-automata work for research and tooling, and describes ltlcross as a rewrite of LBTT that adds PSL support and arbitrary acceptance conditions for testing or benchmarking LTL-to-automata translators. The README does not state a broader motivation beyond that.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the mechanism only at the feature level: formula algorithms (simplification, implication and equivalence checks, stutter-invariance tests, translation to automata) and automata algorithms (products, emptiness checks, simulation-based reduction, determinization, SAT-based minimization, and similar) are exposed through the C++ API and the command-line tools. It supports Emerson-Lei acceptance conditions, and state-based acceptance is handled by reduction to transition-based acceptance. It also covers safety and parity games and reactive synthesis and model checking applications.
brief.install_notes: The homepage links to download and installation instructions, which I did not fetch, so I have no details on build steps or dependencies beyond the fact that it is a C++20 library. The brew description and executable list come from the package metadata, not from a README command. The homepage also mentions an online translator, a Jupyter notebook called spot-sandbox that bundles a full install with the command-line tools and Python bindings, and the mailing lists, but I did not verify those.
brief.standout: Spot covers both LTL and ω-automata with arbitrary Emerson-Lei acceptance conditions, which is less common than tools limited to Büchi or parity acceptance. The command-line tools are Unix-style filters (ltlfilt, autfilt, and so on) that can be piped together, and ltlcross/autcross give a generic way to test or benchmark other translators.
brief.status: Maintained, as far as the homepage shows. It states the latest version is 2.16.1, released 2026-10-16, and links to a current download page. I did not check a commit history or release log, so this is based on the homepage alone.
brief.caveats: Licensed under GNU GPL v3, so any tool that links with Spot must also be distributed under GPL-compatible terms with its source, as the homepage notes. Installation details beyond the C++20 requirement were not read. The brew package has no caveats. The homepage also describes only a subset of the linear fragment of PSL, not full PSL.

judge.reason: Spot makes temporal logic tangible by translating LTL formulas into rich ω-automata, then offering tools to transform, compare, and model-check them.

entry.title: Spot
entry.tldr: A toolkit of Unix-style filters for temporal logic formulas and omega-automata: simplify an LTL formula, turn it into an automaton, test translators against each other.
entry.deeper_look:
Spot is a C++20 library for working with LTL (linear temporal logic) and omega-automata, which are automata that run on infinite sequences. LTL lets you write properties like "every request is eventually answered". Omega-automata are the machines that can check such properties over a system that never stops. Spot reads LTL in several syntaxes plus a subset of the linear fragment of PSL. It reads automata in five formats: HOA, never claims, LBTT, DSTAR and PGsolver.

Most of the algorithms are also exposed as command-line tools, and as Python bindings. The brew package installs 16 executables. Formulas and automata go in, and simplified formulas, translated or transformed automata, test results, benchmark results and synthesis outputs come out. The tools are described as filters that can be piped together, so ltlfilt works on formulas and autfilt works on automata.

The idea underneath is that a logical property and a machine can be the same thing in two forms. Translating a formula into an automaton is the core step in model checking and in reactive synthesis, where a controller is generated from a specification. Spot covers this ground, including safety and parity games and Emerson-Lei acceptance conditions, which is less common than tools limited to Büchi or parity acceptance.

The homepage describes ltlcross as "a rewrite of LBTT, but with support for PSL and automata with arbitrary acceptance conditions". It checks LTL-to-automata translators against each other, which is a good way to see how the field tests its own tools. The homepage also mentions an online translator and a Jupyter notebook called spot-sandbox, but these were not verified.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options of the tool that translates an LTL formula into an automaton.
Shows how to simplify, check and transform LTL formulas read from files or pipes.
Shows the operations available on automata, such as reduction and determinization.

entry.whats_unique: It handles both LTL and omega-automata with arbitrary Emerson-Lei acceptance conditions, through filter-style tools that pipe together. ltlcross and autcross give a generic way to test or benchmark other translators.
entry.caveats: It is GPL v3, so anything linking with the library must be GPL-compatible, and the brief did not cover command examples or build details, so expect to read the documentation.
